faq: What does this tool calculate?
Any one of speed (knots), distance (nautical miles) and time (hours) from the other two — the speed-distance-time triangle in maritime units.
Is it free to use?
Yes — aboard, ashore, in the exam hall's doorway.
How accurate is the result?
Exact arithmetic on your inputs. Real passages add currents, weather and traffic schemes; the triangle gives the plan those corrections amend.
Does the route include live traffic?
The sea has traffic separation schemes rather than traffic jams; neither is in this calculation. It is the pure triangle.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Sea distances follow channels, headlands and great circles rather than roads — measure the passage as sailed and enter that.
Knots — why not km/h?
Because the nautical mile is one minute of latitude, which makes charts and knots a single system. The table on this page converts for landlocked intuition.
Speed through water or over ground?
Enter the one your question uses. GPS reports over ground; logs report through water; passages are planned in whichever, corrected for current.
Average speed versus cruising speed?
Passages average slower than they cruise — ports, pilots and weather take their share. Plan ETAs on the average.
Can it work in km and km/h?
The triangle is unit-agnostic; the maritime dress is knots and nautical miles. Convert with the nautical tools if your vessel thinks metric.
River and canal passages?
Same triangle, lower speeds, plus locks that no formula aboard can hurry. Add lock time as port time.
